DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
## What the author says the study shows

1. The pilot (4,000 households in three mixed wards) shows how Thornbury residents actually behave.
2. Participation was strong, yields were consistent, and 81% of residents rated the service good or very good.
3. Participation held up across houses and flats, so one uniform service can serve the whole district.
4. The financial analysis is complete, and the disposal saving uses real costs.
5. The net cost of about £490,000 is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation of £520,000.
6. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away.
7. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time.

The pilot itself is well designed. Its housing mix (20% flats) matches the district, and measuring participation weekly by housing type is exactly what makes it useful. But the study's own tables contradict claims 3, 5 and 6. The tonnage projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot data. Once that is corrected and Brookfield's capacity limit is applied, the service is no longer shown to be fully funded.

## Arithmetic

**These are correct:**
- Table 1 rates: 2,112/3,200 = 66%, 168/800 = 21%, 2,280/4,000 = 57%. The weighted yield is 1.86 kg, which rounds to 1.9 kg.
- Table 2: 6 vehicles × £165,000 ÷ 7 years = £141,429; 12 operatives × £34,000 = £408,000; the four lines total £733,400.
- Saving per tonne: £112 − £38 = £74. Net cost as stated: £733,400 − £243,000 = £490,400.

**These are wrong:**

**1. Flats participation was not "broadly similar".** It was 21%, against 66% for houses, less than a third of the rate. This is the opposite of what Section 2, the recommendation and the author's description say. The pilot's evidence points toward needing a separate approach for flats, such as communal containers or a different collection arrangement.

**2. The projection uses 64% participation; the pilot measured 57%.** The 64% figure doesn't appear anywhere in Table 1. Applying the pilot's own rates by housing type to the district:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses (80%) | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | 2,713 |
| Flats (20%) | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | 159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **≈ 2,870** |

That is about 2,870 tonnes, not 3,290, so the projection is overstated by about 13%. The pilot's 20% share of flats matches the district's, so these rates should transfer without adjustment.

**3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029.** Even the corrected tonnage exceeds this by about 1,070 tonnes. Section 4 states the limit, but the projection, the savings figure and the author's "treatment is local" all ignore it. The surplus would have to go to the plant 46 miles away, at a gate fee the study doesn't give, plus extra haulage.

## The funding position after correction

| | As stated | Corrected tonnage, all at Brookfield | Corrected tonnage, Brookfield cap applied |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tonnes at £74 saving | 3,290 | 2,870 | 1,800 |
| Disposal saving | £243,000 | £212,500 | £133,200 + saving on surplus (unknown) |
| Net cost | £490,400 | **£520,900** | **up to ~£600,000** |
| Provisional allocation | £520,000 | £520,000 | £520,000 |

Even if the capacity limit is ignored, correcting the participation rate alone takes the net cost slightly over the allocation. With the capacity limit, the shortfall could reach about £80,000 a year, depending on what the second plant charges. The surplus tonnage could even cost more than incineration once haulage is added.

The allocation is also provisional, and the Government has only "indicated" it. "Fully funded" therefore rests on an unconfirmed figure, while the vehicle order commits about £990,000 in December 2026.

## Things the study doesn't establish

- **Whether the incineration saving is real.** The £112 per tonne saving assumes the Council pays per tonne at the margin. If the incineration contract has a fixed fee or a minimum-tonnage clause, diverting food waste may save less, or nothing. Check the contract.
- **Costs that are missing or unclear:**
  - financing costs on the £990,000 vehicle purchase;
  - whether the £34,000 per operative includes employer on-costs;
  - cover for sickness and holidays, since six crews for six vehicles leaves no relief;
  - supervision;
  - the three-month phone line and web page;
  - haulage to the 46-mile plant.
- **How representative the 81% satisfaction figure is.** It comes from "surveyed pilot households". The study doesn't say how many were surveyed or whether non-participants were included. If mostly participants responded, the figure says little about the 43% who didn't take part.
- **Pilot timing.** January to June gives no summer or autumn data, and early enthusiasm for a new service may fade.

## Timetable

The schedule has no slack. Vehicles arrive in March, crews train on them that same month, caddies go to 52,000 households in March, and collections start on 5 April. If the vehicle delivery slips even a few weeks, training and launch slip with it. The study needs a fallback, such as hired vehicles or a phased start.

## Settled and open

**Settled by the study's own figures:**
- Flats participation was 21%, against 66% for houses. A uniform service is not supported by the evidence.
- Projected tonnage is about 2,870, not 3,290.
- Brookfield can treat only 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029.
- On corrected tonnage, the net cost is at or above the £520,000 allocation even before the capacity limit is applied.

**Open, with what would settle each:**
- **Cost of the surplus tonnage:** gate fee and haulage quote from the 46-mile plant.
- **Real disposal saving:** terms of the incineration contract.
- **Funding:** confirmation of the new-burdens allocation, and whether it's tied to a funding formula or to actual costs.
- **Full operating cost:** a revised Table 2 with financing, on-costs, relief staff and supervision.
- **Flats:** a costed alternative approach, ideally tested in a few blocks before April.

## Recommendation for the Cabinet paper

The service is a legal requirement, so the question is how to deliver it, not whether to. Cabinet should still be shown the real position:

1. **Correct Section 3** to use the pilot's measured rates (about 2,870 tonnes).
2. **Correct Section 2** on flats, and add a separate approach for flats.
3. **Rebuild the savings** with Brookfield's cap and a costed plan for the surplus.
4. **Present the funding gap honestly.** On current figures it is a gap of up to ~£80,000 a year, against a provisional allocation.
5. **Add a timetable contingency** for late vehicle delivery.

Authorising the vehicle order may still be the right decision given the April 2027 deadline. It should be presented as a commitment made before funding is confirmed, not as a fully funded one.
